name: Zone diet

card.summary: A 40:30:30 carbohydrate, protein and fat eating plan with portion-based meals that people use to manage body fat and support training, which shapes how lean and muscular they look.
card.note: Reviews describe it as a low-carbohydrate, relatively low-calorie plan; athletes have questioned its fit for heavy training.

quick.overview:
The Zone diet is an eating plan created by American biochemist Barry Sears that targets roughly 40 percent of calories from carbohydrate, 30 percent from protein and 30 percent from fat, spread across three meals and two snacks.

For appearance, the appeal is body composition: followers use it to lose fat while keeping protein steady, and it became popular with some strength and CrossFit athletes. Randomized trials have compared it with other named diets for weight loss, with results generally similar across diets, while sports-nutrition reviews have questioned its performance claims.
quick.how: Followers set a daily protein amount, then build each meal from protein, carbohydrate and fat portions, either by hand-size guides (palm of protein, fist of carbohydrate) or by counting Zone blocks. Meals are spaced no more than about five hours apart, and exercise is encouraged.
quick.risks: Reviews note the plan is low in carbohydrate and can be calorie-restrictive, which has been questioned for endurance and high-volume training. Short-term low-carbohydrate diets can cause fatigue or constipation. People with medical conditions generally discuss changes in diet with a clinician.

lead: The Zone diet is a macronutrient-balancing diet devised by biochemist Barry Sears. It sets calories at about 40 percent carbohydrate, 30 percent protein and 30 percent fat, with protein fixed first and carbohydrate and fat adjusted to energy needs and weight goals.[1]

It is used in physique and fitness circles to reduce body fat while holding muscle. Meals are organised as five eating occasions a day, and portions are tracked with hand-size guides or detailed Zone blocks.[1] Sears's theory is that balancing insulin and glucagon alters eicosanoid production and thereby affects inflammation, performance and weight; reviewers have said this mechanism is unproven.[1][5]

Research includes randomized trials of the Zone against Atkins, Ornish and LEARN diets in overweight women, a JAMA network meta-analysis of named diets, and sports-medicine reviews of the plan for athletes.[3][4][6]

chain: Lower calorie intake and steadier protein
Less body fat with muscle kept, a leaner look
angle.text: Followers use the Zone's fixed protein portions and calorie control to lose fat while keeping muscle. The look comes from the resulting body composition rather than from any effect on the face.

paras: The Zone begins by setting protein needs, then adjusts carbohydrate and fat to energy requirements and weight-loss goals. It is described as a low-carbohydrate approach intended to reduce calorie intake and avoid insulin spikes.[1] A hand-portion guide assigns a palm-sized portion to protein and fist-sized portions to carbohydrate, while the block system allows more detailed tracking with blocks and mini-blocks.[1]

Sports-medicine reviewers note that applying the suggested protein target of about 1.8 to 2.2 g per kg of fat-free mass in practice produces a diet that is low in carbohydrate in relative and absolute terms.[6]

The diet's theory is that a 40:30:30 balance shifts the insulin-to-glucagon ratio, changing eicosanoid metabolism, with claims of lower chronic disease risk, better immunity, better performance, longer life and lasting weight loss.[1] A 2003 review of the Zone phenomenon examined the science behind these claims, placing the diet among the popular modern low-carbohydrate fads.[7] A 1999 sports-medicine review concluded the literature does not support the claim that the diet improves athletic performance or alters pancreatic hormone response.[6]

sections.h: Use in athletics and physique circles
paras: The Zone has been popular among some strength and CrossFit athletes seeking to manage body fat. A 2022 survey examined dietary practices and supplement use among CrossFit participants.[8] Strength-training forum members on T Nation have also mentioned it in training logs and diet threads.

The A TO Z Weight Loss Study (JAMA, 2007) randomized overweight premenopausal women to the Atkins, Zone, Ornish or LEARN diets and compared weight and related risk factors.[3] A 2014 JAMA network meta-analysis of 48 randomized trials with 7,286 participants compared named diets and diet classes for weight loss at 6 and 12 months.[4]

A trial in insulin-resistant obese women compared high-fat and high-protein (Zone-type) diets with a high-carbohydrate diet.[9] A one-week controlled study examined the Zone in recreational endurance athletes, looking at body composition, blood lipids and performance.[10] An Oklahoma trial compared weight loss plans on body composition and duration of diet adherence.[11]

Reviewers note that the calorie level of the Zone can be low for athletes and that high-protein, low-carbohydrate diets typically give short-term weight loss with side effects such as fatigue and constipation.[1][6] A review of fad diets also considered effects on urinary stone formation.[12]
